title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Limitations in current methods


Standard models (For e.g. BART) store their knowledge as model weights during training
Limitations -

Difficult to update without retraining
Hallucinations- model interpolate from compressed parametric memory
There is no way to tell what part was looked at to produce output

This paper treats retrieval as a learnable, differentiable element that can be plugged into a generative model
A jointly trained system where

Model knows what to query
Generator knows how to use what is queried

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Types of Memory



Parametric Memory


Knowledge is frozen into model weights
Can’t update it without retraining
Fast to infer insights but limited and brittle


Non-parametric Memory


Indexed text, external to the model, which the model looks up at runtime
The index can be swapped, updated or replaced independent of model weights

RAG combines both types of memories - retriever fetches relevant documents from non-parametric memory, and generators (that stores parametric knowledge) synthesizes a response using both
Prior work on the hybrid approach was done only on extractive tasks (REALM,ORQA) but RAG extends it to generative seq2seq tasks

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Approach





The paper combines a pre-trained retriever (Query Encoder + Document Index) with a pre-trained seq2seq model (Generator) and fine-tune end-to-end. For query \(x\), we use Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) to find the top-K documents \(z\)\(i\). For final prediction \(y\), we treat \(z\) as a latent variable and marginalize over seq2seq predictions given different documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Methods


The paper explores RAG models, that uses input sequence \(x\) to retrieve text documents \(z\) to use them as additional context when generating the target sequence \(y\)
The model leverages two components

Retriever \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z | x)\) with parameters \(\eta\) that returns top-K truncated distributions over the text given a query \(x\)
Generator \(p\)\(\theta\)(\(y\)i | \(x,z,y\)1:i-1) parametrized by \(\theta\) that generates a current token based on the context of the previous \(i-1\) tokens \(y\)1:i-1 , the original input \(x\) and a retrieved text \(z\)

The retrieved documents are treated as latent variable - the model never directly supervises which document is correct
The paper proposes two models - RAG-Sequence that uses the same document to predict each target token and RAG-Token which can predict each target token based on a different document

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Sequence Model


uses the same retrived document to generate complete sequence
treats retrieved document as a single latent variable marginalized to get seq2seq probability \(p(y|x)\) via a top-K approximation
top K documents are retrived using the retriver and generator produces output sequence probability of each document, then marginalized



\(p\)RAG-Sequence\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) \(=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




\(\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\) is the standard autoregressive generator
\(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) does it for top-K documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Token Model


Draw different latent document for each target token
Allows the generator to choose content from different documents when generating a response
Once top K documents are retrieved, the generator produces a distribution for the next output token for each document, before marginalizing
The process is repeated for following output token




\(p\)RAG-Token\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Models


RAG-Token Model




\(p\)RAG-Token\((y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




The product is outside while the sum is inside, compared to RAG Sequence. At each token position \(i\), the model considers all K documents simultaneously, weights each document’s contribution to this specific token by the retrieval probability, and sums.
Then moves to position \(i+1\) and does it again — potentially with a different document dominating.
RAG can be used for sequence classification tasks by considering target class as a target sequence of length one, where RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Retriever


The retriever \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) is based on Dense Passage Retrival (DPR) that follows a bi-encoder structure




\(d(z)\) = BERT\(d\)\((z)\) document encoder
\(q(x)\) = BERT\(q\)\((x)\) query encoder



with a retrival probability of



\(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\) \(\propto\) exp \((d(z)^T.q(x))\)




Higher dot product equals higher probability of retrival
Finding top-K is a Maximum Inner Product Search problem
Solved approximately using FAISS + HNSW graphs - sub-linear time over 21 million documents

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Retriever


One performace tradeoff is that the Document Encoder \(d(z)\) is frozen during fine-tuning

Re-embedding 21 million documents every training step is expensive
The initialization DPR retriever was pre-trained specifically to retrieve passages relevant to Natural Questions and TriviaQA. This means the document embeddings it produces are already semantically well-organized
So \(d(z)\) already has a meaningful embedding space before fine-tuning begins
Doesn’t hurt the performance significantly
Prevents catastrophic indexing - Updating the encoded during training changes the embedding, clashing with FAISS which was build over old embeddings

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Generator


400M parameter seq2seq transformer, pre-trained with a denoising objective
Input is simply the concatenation of query and retrieved document: [\(x\) ; \(z\)]
Generates answer autoregressively, one token at a time:




\(p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)




At each step: conditioned on the full query, the retrieved document, and all prior output tokens
BART over T5:

BART outperforms comparably-sized T5 on generation tasks
Bidirectional encoder + left-to-right decoder is well-suited for this hybrid input structure

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Marginalizing Over Documents


Since the “correct” document is unknown, both RAG variants sum (marginalize) over top-K documents, weighted by retrieval probability




RAG-Sequence has the same document for the whole output

Generates a complete answer for each document, then weight by how likely it was to be retrieved



\(p(y|x)=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x)\prod p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)


RAG-Token potentially has different document per output token

At each token step, the model can draw from a different document



\(p(y|x)\) \(\approx\) \(\prod_{i}^{N}\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) . p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z,y\)1:i-1 \()\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Training


Trained end-to-end on input/output pairs (\(x\)\(j\),\(y\)\(j\) ) only — no supervision on which document to retrieve
Loss function: negative marginal log-likelihood of the target output

\(Loss\) = - \(\sum\)\(j\) \(log\) \(p(y\)\(j\)|\(x\)\(j\) \()\)

Gradient flows through BART (generator) and the query encoder
The system learns to retrieve by learning what helps it generate correct answers
Only the query encoder and BART are updated; document encoder + index are frozen
Optimizer: Adam with stochastic gradient descent

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Token

Per-token probability factors are plugged directly into standard beam decoder
Transition probability


\(p'\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,y\)1:i-1 \()\) \(=\) \(\sum_{z\in top-k(p(.|x))}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z\)\(i\)\(|x)p\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,z\)\(i\)\(,y\)1:i-1 \()\)


To decode, \(p'\)\(\theta\)\((y\)i\(|x,y\)1:i-1 \()\) can be plugged into a standard beam decoder

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Sequence

Full sequence probability \(p(y|x)\) doesn’t factor per-token, hence can’t do a single beam search
Thorough Decoding:

Get \(K\) sets of candidate sequences by running beam search independently for each of the \(K\) retrieved documents

Take the union of all candidates across all K beams which is the hypothesis set \(Y\)
For any candidate \(y\) that didn’t appear in a particular document’s beam, run an additional forward pass through BART to score it against that document anyway
Final probability

\(p(y|x)=\) \(\sum_{z}\) \(p\)\(\eta\)\((z|x) . p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) summed across all \(K\) documents

Pick the highest scoring \(y\)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Decoding


RAG-Sequence

Fast Decoding

Similar to Thorough, but skips Step 3
If a candidate was generated from document 1’s beam but not document 2’s, Thorough Decoding still need to score it against document 2. With K=10 and a large hypothesis set, this is computinally expensive
In Fast Decoding, if \(y\) didn’t appear in document \(z\)’s beam, \(p\)\(\theta\)\((y|x,z)\) is assumed as 0

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Experiments

RAG was tested across five distinct task types to prove generality:

Open-Domain QA (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, WebQuestions, CuratedTrec) — exact match
Abstractive QA (MS-MARCO) — free-form answer generation, BLEU + Rouge-L
Jeopardy Question Generation — given an entity, generate the Jeopardy clue — Q-BLEU-1 + human evaluation
Fact Verification (FEVER) — classify claims as supported / refuted / not enough information

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Ablations


Frozen vs. learned retrieval:

RAG-Token with frozen retriever: 37.8 on NQ and 43.5 with learned
Learning to retrieve is worth ~6 EM points on NQ alone

Dense retrieval (DPR) vs. sparse retrieval (BM25):

BM25 replacement tanks QA performance significantly (29.7 vs. 43.5 on NQ for RAG-Token)
Exception: FEVER — BM25 performs comparably or better, because fact-checking claims are entity-heavy and keyword overlap is a reliable signal
For generation tasks: dense retrieval is crucial

Number of retrieved documents:

RAG-Sequence: more docs monotonically helps QA
RAG-Token: performance peaks at K=10, then levels off
Flexibility to adjust K at inference time without retraining is a practical advantage

RAG’s world knowledge lives in the index, not the weights, and hence a deplyed RAG system can be updated on factual knowledge by replacing its document store

without retraining

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Generation vs Extraction


All four QA benchmarks in the paper are classified as extractive tasks — the answer exists verbatim in some document.
Still, RAG’s generative approach beats purpose-built extractive systems.

Documents that contain clues but not the verbatim answer can still guide generation — extraction can’t use them at all
Marginalization over \(K\) documents lets multiple partial-evidence documents contribute to a single correct answer
Generation can synthesize across documents while extraction is limited to one span in one document
RAG can produce correct answers even when no retrieved document contains the answer

The non-parametric memory being raw text (not embeddings) is a design choice
Keeps the memory human-readable and human-writable
Gives you authority to correct - a factual error can be corrected by editing a document in the index, the same thing cannot be done with weights

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Limitations


Single knowledge source (Wikipedia was the one source tested)
Joint pre-training wasn’t explored, only fine-tuning. was performed
RAG-Sequencing Decoding doesn’t scale optimally
Knowledge spanning multiple documents can’t be multi-hopped while reasoning natively
No inference regarding when to retrieve vs. when to rely purely on parametric memory

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Legacy of the Paper

While some of the specific components have been replaced by stronger alternatives, the core ideas from this paper propel the field even today

Treat retrieval as a learnable, differentiable function
Marginalize over uncertainty in which document is relevant
Separate updatable knowledge (index) from reasoning capability (weights)
Train end-to-end on (input, output) pairs without document-level supervision
Hot-Swapping has saved retraining costs across the industry- The observation that a 400M parameter model with a good index beats an 11B parameter model without one reshaped how to think about the scaling-vs-retrieval tradeoff

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text:
Current Advances


Retrievers

Sparse + Dense Hybrid Retrievals outperform and have replaced DPR
Both encoders can be fine-tuned using. contrastive learning, solving the frozen document-encoder compromise

Generators

BART has been replaced by stronger LLMs like LLaMA, Mistral, GPT-4
Capability to synthesize retrieved context has improved

Multi-Hop RAG

Modern systems reads retrieved docs, generates a sub-question, retrieves again, and chains reasoning across multiple retrieval steps

Production RAG

The index hot-swap insight became the architectural backbone of virtually every enterprise AI system — LlamaIndex, LangChain, and similar frameworks are essentially RAG pipelines with better chunking, re-ranking, and hybrid retrieval layered on top

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
section: Limitations in current methods of variant interpretation
text:
Limitations in current methods of variant interpretation

Traditional penetrance estimates rely on small, disease-enriched cohorts → ascertainment bias
Patients are classified in a binary manner - case/control, sick/healthy, etc. while ignoring the fact that diseases exist on a spectrum
Studies with smaller scope cannot assess rare variants with significant accuracy
Difficult to interpret if Variants of Uncertain Signifance (VUS) are associated with disease pathogenecity or are harmful

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Research Question


Given a genetic variant exists in a patient, can machine learning and statistical methods predict what is its penetrance?

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
ML Penetrance Evaluation


Apply ML models to generate continuous disease probability scores (0-1)
Use Generalized Linear Mixed-Effects Model (GLMM) to compute penetrance
Accounts for variability between carriers and across ML iterations

logit-transformed disease scores from all 50 ML iterations in all carriers, which accounted for variability in scores between different carriers (random effects term) and variability in scores between different ML iterations within the same individual (residual random effects term)
The model’s inverse logit coefficients and error terms were then used to provide a point estimate of ML penetrance, 95% confidence interval (95% CI), and p-value

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Clinical Applications


Improved Variant Classification: Quantitative risk estimates beyond P/LP/VUS categories
Enhanced Risk Stratification: Individualized screening protocols based on ML penetrance
Genetic Counseling: More precise risk communication to patients
Clinical Trial Recruitment: Identify high-penetrance variant carriers
Resource Allocation: Prioritize monitoring for high-risk individuals

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Study Strengths


Large-scale: >1.3 million participants with deep phenotyping
Unselected population: Reduced ascertainment bias vs. family studies
Quantitative: Continuous penetrance estimates, not binary
Clinically grounded: Uses routine lab data already in EHR
Validated: Functional data, clinical outcomes, external cohorts
High-throughput: Scalable to other health systems and diseases

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Limitations & Future Directions

Limitations:

Dependent on EHR data quality and completeness
Focused on autosomal dominant conditions
Limited diversity in training cohorts
Does not address genetic modifiers or environmental factors

Future Work:

Extend to other inheritance patterns and rare diseases
Develop ancestry-specific models
Prospective studies following variant carriers longitudinally
Integration with functional assays and polygenic risk scores

title: Machine Learning-Based Penetrance of Genetic Variants
text:
Key Takeaways


ML-based penetrance provides refined, quantitative disease risk estimates for genetic variants
ML penetrance correlates with clinical outcomes and functional data, validating biological relevance
Enables interpretation of VUS and LoF variants through clinical trajectory analysis
Represents a scalable blueprint for precision medicine using routine EHR data

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Hypertension

Hypertension is the leading modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease
~7.8 million deaths worldwide in 2015 were attributable to high blood pressure
Hypertension is a polygenic disease that is driven by many genomic variants, not one
Genomic risk is only one factor, along with lifestyle, environment, and other comorbidities, but this paper focuses primarily on the genomic components

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
section: Approaches used to find genomic risk variants
text:
Approaches used to find genomic risk variants

The state of the art method of identifying genomic risk variants is Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS)
GWAS identify variant-trait associations at a population level, testing each SNP via Logistic regression or Fisher’s exact test with genome-wide signficance at p \(< 5 x 10^{-8}\)
GWAS takes a large population, split into cases vs. controls
Visualization is commonly done with a Manhattan plot

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Limitations of GWAS

Needs huge sample sizes (~1 million people) to detect low-frequency variants especially those with low minor allele frequency (MAF)
The ~1,000 known BP loci explain only ~5.7% of the genetic variance in blood pressure
Most detected SNPs are common, small-effect variants
GWAS can answer questions like what is the population-level risk of a particular variant? but it cannot answer questions like what is the risk of a particular variant for a specific patient?







Important


A given hypertensive patient may carry none of the population’s significant risk alleles

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Core Idea

Instead of researching “what matters for the average patient?”, the goal is to observe “what matters for patients who share this specific variant with me?”


IBI models each variant’s effect in the subpopulation that actually carries it
Builds on TCI (tumor-specific causal inference), originally developed for individual cancer genomes
IBI aims to identify personalized, potentially causal genomic drivers of a trait, beyond just population-average associations

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Building Block: Bayesian Networks



IBI uses a bipartite Bayesian Network (BN) with two node sets-

Set 1: Variants \(V\) (e.g., SNPs)
Set 2: Traits \(T\) (e.g., hypertension)

Directed edges \(V -> T\) represent probabilistic dependency with only one assumed influencing variant being evaluated at a time indicated by solid arc
Network structures are scored using the Bayesian Dirichlet equivalent uniform (BDeu) score that tells you how well a proposed structure is supported by the data





Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Population-level Bayesian Scoring using GWAS



For variant \(V_s\) and trait \(T_i\) over the full population \(D\), the marginal likelihood \(P(D \mid V_s \to T_i)\) (log form: \(M_s\)) is computed
Under an uniform prior, ranking by \(M_s\) is proportional to ranking by global posterior probability, and is directly comparable to GWAS’s p-value ranking





Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Individualizing Step



For a given patient \(h\) who carries the minor allele of
\(V_s\) (\(V_s = 1\))

Partition the population into \(D^{V_s=1}\) (“patients-like-me,” carrying the variant) and \(D^{V_s=0}\) (everyone else)
Score \(V_s\)’s ability to explain Hypertension within \(D^{V_s=1}\) -> \(M_s^1\)
Find the variant \(V_r\) that best explains the remaining group \(D^{V_s=0}\) -> \(M_r^0\)
Combine: \(M_{s,r} = M_s^1 + M_r^0\) This overall score, \(M_{s,r}\), is higher than the single-population estimator’s score (\(M_s\) using one global variant \(V_g\)) for many SNPs, because two distinct, subgroup-specific explanations together can fit the data better than one global explanation






Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network





One variant explains “people like this patient.” A second explains everyone else. Together they almost always beat the single best population-wide variant

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Personalized posterior probability




For each patient, \(M_{s,r}\) is normalized across only the minor-allele SNPs present in that individual’s genome, yielding an individualized posterior probability \(P(V_s^h \to T_i^h \mid D)\)
The same SNP can therefore rank differently across patients depending on their distinct genomic backgrounds
The highest-ranked variant for a patient is IBI’s proposed individualized explanation of their HTN status







Fig 1. Variants (\(V\)) -> Traits (\(T\)): a bipartite Bayesian network

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
The Cohort: Framingham Heart Study

Cohort: Framingham Heart Study (FHS), Affymetrix HuGeneFocused50K genotyping array (dbGaP phs000007.v30.p11)
QC: --mind 0.03 --geno 0.03 --maf 0.01 --hwe 10e-6 --me 0.05 0.1 --sexCheck gives 38,342 SNPs

After removing minor-allele risk ratio < 1, final count= 19,276 SNPs

Linkage Disequilibrium (LD) pruning: d′ threshold 0.2 (SNPRelate) reduces it to 19,006 SNPs (98.5% independent)
Final analytic sample: 6,613 patients
Split: 80% discovery (5,290) / 20% held-out test (1,323)

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Defining “Hypertension”
A patient is coded HTN = 1 if:

Systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg, or
Diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg, or
Currently on antihypertensive medication (+10 mmHg SBP / +5 mmHg DBP correction applied if on treatment, per TOPMed harmonization)

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Comparison

Fig 2. A Bayesian method for GWAS analysis
Population-level \(M_s\) and GWAS p-values are highly concordant
Spearman ρ = −0.90; 164/189 top independent SNPs and 18/20 top-5-ranked SNPs overlap between rankings
This establishes that the Bayesian framework reproduces GWAS when used non-individually, before the individualizing extension is applied

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
section: IBI vs. GWAS: variant discovery (discovery set, n=5,290)
text:
IBI vs. GWAS: variant discovery (discovery set, n=5,290)




GWAS (Bonferroni α = 0.05/19,276 = 2.59×10⁻⁶): 5 SNPs reach significance
IBI: 189 SNPs exceed the population-level best-estimator’s \(M_s\) (i.e., a two-subgroup explanation beats the single best global explanation)
Overlap: 40 of the top-189 SNPs shared between IBI and GWAS (agreement); 148 unique to one or the other (complementarity)
MAF distribution: IBI-only SNPs have markedly lower MAF than GWAS-only SNPs. IBI’s individualized partitioning better surfaces rare-variant signal
Information gain (IG): IG for IBI’s top-189 SNPs > GWAS’s top-189 SNPs > 189 random SNPs (all comparisons directionally consistent with expectation)










Fig 3. Manhattan plots: IBI’s normalized \(M_{s,r}\) (A) vs. GWAS p-values (B)

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Patient-Level Explanation


GWAS, using population-significant SNPs

Only 16 unique SNPs ever serve as a patient’s top explanatory variant
Only 12.9% of HTN patients carry a Bonferroni-significant SNP
Even with relaxed threshold, only 15.7% covered


IBI

25 unique SNPs serve as top-1 explanatory variants (more diverse coverage)
99.1% of HTN patients get a top SNP with posterior probability ≥ 0.10
79.7% still covered at a stricter threshold of 0.20



Average patient carries 7,767 minor-allele SNPs (of 19,276)
Under a naive uniform prior this implies ~1.3×10⁻⁴ per-SNP prior probability
IBI’s assigned posterior probabilities (0.08–0.99 range for top SNP) are far above this baseline



That’s the clinical gap this paper is trying to close — most hypertensive patients simply don’t carry a “significant” population-level variant

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Spotlight: One SNP, 425 Patients

Intronic SNP rs13265032 in the CSMD1 locus
Assigned as the top explanatory variant for 46% (425/930) of HTN patients by IBI
Ranked 12th by IBI’s own scoring which implies a real signal, not noise
Ranked 5,361st by GWAS — essentially invisible to standard analysis
CSMD1 variants have been independently linked to BP and hydrochlorothiazide response in prior literature

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Strengths of the Study

Direct, apples-to-apples comparison against GWAS in the same cohort
Multiple independent lines of evidence: overlap analysis, information gain, MAF distribution, literature cross-checks, held-out prediction
Fully reproducible: code and summary data are public on GitHub
Grounded in a well-characterized, real longitudinal cohort (Framingham)


~30–45 sec.

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Questions & Limitations

Does not yet adjust for age, sex, population structure, or family relatedness (planned: linear mixed models)
Associations are not necessarily causal, they are confounded by LD and population structure
AUROC improvement (0.55 → 0.59–0.60) is real but modest
Single cohort (FHS), genotyping array rather than whole-genome sequencing
“Patients-like-me” subgroup size can be very small for rare variants and stability of these estimates is worth scrutinizing

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Next steps

Extend to whole-genome sequencing data (rare variants are IBI’s sweet spot)
Generalize beyond discrete traits to continuous traits (swap BDeu → BIC score) — e.g., lipid levels, continuous BP
Incorporate linear mixed models for population structure / relatedness
Search for combinations of variants acting jointly, not just one at a time
Fine-mapping / functional validation / Mendelian randomization to move from association toward causation

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Key Messages

GWAS finds what matters on average — not necessarily what matters for the patient in front of you
IBI reframes variant discovery around the individual’s genomic background, by scoring a “patients-like-me” subgroup separately from everyone else
In the Framingham cohort, IBI explained far more hypertensive patients (99% vs. 16%), surfaced biologically plausible rare variants GWAS missed, and gave a modest but significant boost in predictive accuracy

text:
Bayesian Networks & Bayesian Inference


Bayesian network: a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where nodes are random variables and edges encode probabilistic (and candidate causal) dependencies. The joint distribution factorizes along the graph
Bayesian inference: updating a prior belief about a hypothesis with observed data (via the likelihood) to get a posterior belief using Bayes’ rule

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Marginal Likelihood & Bayesian Scoring

Marginal likelihood \(P(D \mid \text{model})\): the probability of the observed data, integrating out uncertainty in the model’s parameters. This is used to compare candidate network structures without overfitting to one parameter setting
BDeu score (Bayesian Dirichlet equivalent uniform): a closed-form marginal likelihood for discrete variables with a uniform structural prior. In this study, IBI uses BDeu for binary HTN status
BIC (Bayesian information criterion): a large-sample approximation to marginal likelihood, applicable to continuous variables. Under future work, the authors’ proposed swap-in for continuous traits like lipid levels would need to use BIC

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Individualized Causal Inference



A family of methods that estimate a model specific to one instance (a patient, a tumor) rather than a single model averaged over the whole population — by partitioning the population into an instance-relevant subgroup and its complement, then combining subgroup-specific explanations.

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
DAGs & the Causal Markov Condition


Directed acyclic graph (DAG):

nodes = variables
directed edges = direct dependence, no directed cycles

Causal Markov condition:

Each node is independent of its non-descendants, given its direct parents. This lets the joint distribution factorize into local pieces

IBI’s own graph is deliberately minimal and it is designed as bipartite, and only one edge \(V_s \to T_i\) evaluated at a time. It never learns a structure with multiple parents pointing into \(T\)

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Faithfulness — and IBI’s Consistency Claim

Faithfulness: every conditional independence present in the data-generating distribution is a consequence of the graph’s structure (via d-separation) and is not a coincidental cancellation of two or more paths’ effects


Faithfulness is what makes learning causal structure from observational data alone possible at all
Not explicitly tested in this paper: Genomic data is a plausible place for near-violations: strong linkage disequilibrium can produce highly correlated or near-cancelling signals between nearby SNPs, where faithfulness condition may not hold

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Confounding: LD & Population Structure


Confounding: a third variable that influences both the “exposure” (a SNP) and the “outcome” (HTN), creating a spurious or inflated association
Linkage disequilibrium (LD): nearby SNPs are correlated, so a flagged SNP may just be “riding along” with the true causal variant
Population structure: ancestry differences can independently affect both allele frequencies and disease prevalence, inflating spurious associations — this is exactly why the authors flag it as unmodeled in the current IBI implementation

section: Hypertension causal structure is more complex than IBI’s Arc
text:
Hypertension causal structure is more complex than IBI’s Arc
IBI evaluates a single arc \(V_s \to T_i\). The true system generating hypertension almost certainly has more structure behind it, including



LD / haplotype fork: SNPs that operate close together are generally inherited together on the same ancestral chromosome segment

A latent haplotype block \(H\) can be a common cause of two correlated SNPs
One or more SNPs may just “ride along” with the true causal variant

Collider risk in case-control conditioning:

Patient-Coverage results analyze only within the Hypertension patients hence bringing means implicitly conditioning on the trait
If two variants each independently influence HTN, that would be a collider, and conditioning on HTN status can induce a spurious association between them that wouldn’t exist population-wide

title: An Individualized Bayesian Method for Estimating Genomic Variants of Hypertension
text:
Information Gain
Information gain (IG): the reduction in uncertainty (entropy) about the outcome (HTN status) once you know a variant’s genotype
\[IG(T; V) = H(T) - H(T \mid V)\] - \(H(T)\): entropy of HTN status before knowing anything about the variant. - \(H(T \mid V)\): remaining entropy after conditioning on the variant’s genotype

A variant that perfectly separates cases from controls has high IG; a variant unrelated to HTN has IG ≈ 0
Used in the paper as an independent check that IBI-selected SNPs are more informative about HTN than GWAS-selected or random SNPs

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Limitations in current methods


Diseases and conditions don’t happen in  isolation  - they cluster and affect each other’s progression
Current risk prediction methods operate in silos, concentrating on  one condition  at a time
In most patients with intensive health burden, for e.g. aging populations, better models are required to represent the complexity of multiple diseases and their progression

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
section: Mapping human history as a large language model (LLM)
text:
Mapping human history as a large language model (LLM)


LLMs, like ChatGPT and Claude, use statistical models to predict the next word in a sentence based on the previous words
The paper hypothesizes that a similar approach can be applied to disease progression, where past diagnoses can be used to predict future ones
Diseases are “words,” a patient’s health history is a “sentence”

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
GPT-2 vs Delphi-2M








GPT-2 (Original)
Delphi-2M (Modified)




Discrete positional encoding
Continuous age encoding (sine/cosine)


Predicts next token only
Also predicts time to next event (exponential model)


Standard causal masking
Masks same-time tokens (no circular causality)




Model size: 2.2 million parameters (12 layers, 12 heads, 120-dim embedding)
Follows empirical scaling laws — performance improves with more data

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Results and Discussion


Performed significantly well across ~1,000 diseases
Average AUC ~0.76 across all diseases in internal validation
97% of diagnoses had AUC > 0.5 (better than random)
Predicting death: AUC = 0.97
Performance holds up to 10 years into the future (AUC ~0.70)

Compared to current standards:

Matches or beats cardiovascular risk scores (Framingham, QRisk3)
Matches dementia risk scores (UKBDRS)
Outperforms death prediction tools (Charlson, Elixhauser)

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Results and Discussion


For a patient with digestive tract diseases → pancreatic cancer risk elevated 19×
Pancreatic cancer diagnosis → mortality rate elevated ~93,000×
Chickenpox peaks in childhood; heart attacks rise exponentially with age
Delphi updates each person’s risk every time a new diagnosis is recorded

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Clinical and Biological Revalence


Unlike conventional models, Delphi can sample entire future health trajectories
Input: everything known about a patient up to age 60
Output: simulated health events for the next 20 years
Applications:

Estimating future disease burden at population scale
Planning healthcare resources for specific communities
Identifying who needs screening before conventional age thresholds

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Clinical and Biological Revalence


Early Cancer or any disease screenings
Clinical Decision Support by including multi-disease risk
Predicting community-level disease burden for healthcare planning
Digital Twin technology and Similar Patient identification for personalized medicine

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Limitations


Only predicts correlations, not causations
Limited performance for ages 80+ (insufficient training data)
Diabetes prediction still outperformed by a single blood biomarker (HbA1c)
UK Biobank population is skewed towards white, affluent, educated — the healthy volunteer bias
Recruitment ages are between 40-70 years old and hence underestimates early mortality (immortality bias)
Data source missingness (hospital vs. GP records) influences predictions

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Future Directions


Add genomic data, imaging, wearables, prescription records
Connect Delphi to LLMs as a risk module
Integration of free-text clinical notes

If interested, you can also read Dr. Yonghui Wu’s thoughts on the paper in Nature

title: Learning the Natural History of Human Disease with Generative Transformers
text:
Information Modelling Context


Based on the study, results and limitations presented by the researchers, they use the phrase AI very carefully (less than 10 times in the paper text)
A rational understanding of Delphi will validate the same - there is nothing artificially intelligent about it
It is a statistical model that learns patterns in data and makes predictions based on those patterns
The part that seperates it from other similar studies is their implmentation of disease history modelling as the input for their model, representing events in a time-series, generalizable to any patient in any common data model (For e.g. i2b2, OMOP, PCORNET, etc.)
Fixed coordinate systems are not a new concept- principles of genetic data analysis are build on genomic coordinates that are uniform across all patients, and hence it is easier to identify mutations and changes and make inferences about their effects on disease risk and progression
Similarly, the use of age as a coordinate system for disease history allows for a more standardized and interpretable representation of health trajectories, which can be applied across different patient populations and healthcare settings
